extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, astronomers, and readers of Newtonian celestial-mechanical theory
extracted.subtask_description: Derivations and applied methods from Newton's Principia for computing lunar inclination, tidal forces, lunar figure, precession of the equinoxes, comet distances, and cometary motion; includes worked numerical examples and observational comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method to find inclination of the lunar orbit (Prop. XXXV, Prob. XV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a time, construct geometric relations (AD = sine of maximum inclination, AB = sine of minimum inclination, bisect BD at C, describe circle BGD, take CE in AC in ratio to EB as EB to 2BA, set angle AEG equal to twice the distance of the nodes from quadrature, drop perpendicular GH to AD), and then AH is the sine of the sought inclination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposition shows AH (the sine of the inclination sought) equals GE^2 expressed as GH^2 + HE^2 and then algebraically reduced to 2·EC·AH; thus with 2·EC given, GE^2 is proportional to AH. Use the construction where angle AEG equals twice the nodes' distance from quadrature; AH varies with the sine of that angle so as nodes move AH remains equal when G coincides with B or D. Numerical examples and corollaries show how to compute the total hourly variation and present numerical inclination values (e.g., mediocris inclination ~5°8'½ in one case, adjustments to 5°17'46" when nodes in syzygies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Computation of the Sun's tidal force on the sea (Prop. XXXVI, Prob. XVI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute the Sun's force on the sea by comparing the perturbing solar force (ML or PS) to local gravity using earlier propositions, adjust for distance from Earth's center to surface (diminution by ratio ≈60½), and combine contributions from regions 90° from the Sun (depression) and subsolar/antisolar regions (elevation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using earlier results the solar perturbing force in quadratures is given as to gravity roughly 1 to 638092.6; doubled in syzygies. Reducing to the Earth's surface (factor ~60.5) gives ≈1:38,604,600; the two opposite contributions sum to yield a total solar tidal effect ∼1:12,868,200 of gravity. From that, Newton computes the resulting sea-height differences (corollary: solar effect alone would change sea level by about one Parisian foot and eleven Parisian fingers between sub-solar/anti-solar regions and regions 90° from the Sun). The proposition shows how inverse-square scaling and geometric placement produce the net effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of the Moon's tidal force from observations (Prop. XXXVII, Prob. XVII)
rubrics_metrics.description: Infer the Moon's tidal force by comparing observed tidal amplitudes at different lunar phases (syzygy vs quadrature) at measured locations (e.g., Avon near Bristol and Plymouth) and solving the ratio relations between solar and lunar contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton uses observed total rise (≈45 ft in syzygies) and rise in quadratures (≈25 ft) to form equations relating S (solar force) and L (lunar force), adjusting lunar effect for declination via the square of the sine of the complement of declination (numerical factor ~0.91706). Two observational datasets give different L:S ratios (≈57/15 ≈ 3.8 and ≈7.33:1); Newton adopts an intermediate value ~6⅓:1 and derives lunar force ≈1:2,031,821 of gravity. The proposition discusses uncertainties, sensitivity to ocean geometry, and local amplification (ports, narrow passages), and warns that better observations are needed to refine the ratio.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of tidal amplitude dependence on ocean geometry (Corollaries to Prop. XXXVII)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tidal amplitude depends strongly on the breadth, depth, and configuration of the sea and coasts: wide, deep oceans (longitude extent ≳90°) produce larger tides; narrow or shallow seas produce smaller tides; funneling in bays and estuaries can greatly amplify local tides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton discusses examples (Pacific vs Atlantic vs Æthiopic seas), ports (Plymouth, Chepstow, St. Michael's, Auranches, Cambai and Pegu) where shallow approaches or constricted channels amplify tides to many feet, and the opposite effect where open, steep littoral drop produces tides closer to the tidal forcing predicted by solar and lunar forces. This is presented as explanatory guidance when comparing theoretical tidal forcing with observed amplitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using tidal forces to infer lunar density, mass, and surface gravity (Corollaries 3–5, Prop. XXXVII)
rubrics_metrics.description: Relate the relative strengths of lunar and solar tidal forces (and apparent angular diameters) to infer relative densities and masses: from L:S and apparent diameters infer density ratios, then derive mass and surface gravity ratios of Moon and Earth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because tidal forces scale as (density × apparent_diameter^3) (Newton's formulation: forces ∝ densities × cubes of apparent diameters inversely), combining L:S ≈ 6⅓:1 with apparent angular diameters (Sun ≈31'27", Moon ≈32'12") leads Newton to density estimates (Sun : Moon ≈34:5) and then density Moon : Earth ≈9:5, giving mass Moon : Earth ≈1:26 and lunar surface gravity approximately half Earth's. The corollary states the assumptions and numerical steps; Newton warns observational uncertainties and chooses intermediate proportions when observations disagree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference of the Moon's figure from tidal equilibrium (Prop. XXXVIII)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Moon were fluid and distorted by Earth's tidal force analogously to Earth's oceans, compute the equilibrium figure (prolate spheroid with major axis directed toward Earth) and deduce that the same face of the Moon must continually face Earth (synchronous rotation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton sets up proportionalities comparing Earth's tidal effect on a fluid Moon and the Moon's tidal effect on Earth's seas: with the mass/diameter ratios he derives a ratio leading to an estimate that, were the lunar fluid body free, the maximum diameter through the Earth would exceed perpendicular diameters by ~180 Paris feet. Thus the Moon would adopt a spheroidal shape with the same face toward Earth; any oscillations back from that orientation would be very slow because the disturbing forces are small. The proposition gives numeric ratios (e.g., 65:9) used in the estimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computation of the precession of the equinoxes from solar (and lunar) torques (Prop. XXXIX, Prob. XIX)
rubrics_metrics.description: Model Earth's outer matter as an annulus (or concentric elliptic shells) acted on by solar and lunar forces that cause regression of the equinoctial points; combine nodal motions, annulus-to-globe mass ratios (from Lemmas), and geometric corrections (inclination sine-complement) to compute the annual precession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton computes the mean hourly motion of the lunar nodes in a circular orbit (when nodes are in quadratures), converts to annual values, then relates annulus motions to Earth's rotation via ratios of masses and moments (see Lem. II). Accounting for the way distributed mass reduces the effective torque (Lemma I) and correcting for obliquity (multiply by sin complement ≈0.91706), he derives a theoretical annual regression close to observed (computed ≈49"58' per year, observational ≈50"). He further shows adding the lunar contribution (L vs S) changes the result proportionally (e.g., scaling by about 7⅓:1), producing the stated value (numerical steps and ratios are presented in detail).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of Earth's internal mass distribution on precession (Lemmas I–III)
rubrics_metrics.description: The regression of the equinoxes depends on how Earth's mass is distributed (concentrated toward center vs equator). If mass is spread in annular or concentric elliptic shells, the torques and resulting precession rates change by computable ratios; model the Earth as combinations of shells to compute the net effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemma I shows that the effective torque from all exterior particles (above a reference spheroid) is one-quarter less than it would be for the same mass placed uniformly in the equator. Lemma II derives ratios between rotation rates of cylinders, spheres, and thin annuli based on moments and areas; Lemma III states that an annulus rotating and also revolving about the Sun has the same motion of its equinoctial points whether fluid or rigid. Use these lemmas to convert mass distribution into multiplicative factors affecting precession; Newton provides specific numeric ratios (e.g., factors like 4143:443391 and others) for his Earth model and shows how varying the assumed density distribution changes the precession estimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inferring comet distances and orbits from parallactic behaviour, apparent motion, and brightness (Lemma IV and related discussion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the parallactic component of an observed comet's apparent motion (the component arising from Earth's motion) and measured angular differences between successive observations to deduce the comet's distance; supplement parallax analysis with brightness and apparent-diameter scaling (inverse-square for illumination and inverse for apparent diameter) and behaviour of tails to constrain whether comets lie within planetary regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton sets up a geometric construction: from three observed longitudes and times, construct line AB and extend to G so that AG:AB = time(first→last):time(first→second); join QG etc. The angle between predicted and observed longitudes at the last observation gives the parallactic angle, from which distance in the ecliptic plane is deduced. He also uses micrometric measures of apparent diameters and relative luminosities (examples from Flamsteed, Hevelius, Cysat) to argue that comets are usually interior to or within planetary regions (often below Saturn) because their apparent brightness and measured diameters scale with that hypothesis. Newton warns about obscuration by cometary coma/fumes and tail-light scattering; these factors can bias brightness-based distance estimates. Examples with numeric diameter/brightness ratios are given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keplerian motion of comets: conic sections and equal-area law (Prop. XL, Theor. XXI and Corollary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comets move in conic sections (with the Sun at a focus) and sweep out areas proportional to times (equal areas in equal times). Periodic comets follow elliptical orbits and their periods relate to axis lengths as for planets (periods ∝ (axis)^(3/2) — stated as the sesquialtera ratio of transverse axes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton asserts the law by reference to earlier propositions (Prop. XIII of Book I and Props. VIII, XII, XIII of Book III) and provides the immediate corollary: if comets return to their orbits they are ellipses and their periodic times relate to planetary periods by the sesquialtera (3/2) power of the transverse axes. Use equal-area construction to relate observed angular motion to time elapsed along the orbit.
